positions.thesis: Held flat at the top weight because nothing changed in the price and everything changed for the better in the facts. Since my fill Pfizer raised FY26 revenue guidance by $500m at the midpoint on oncology and Eliquis strength, announced $2.5bn of incremental productivity savings through 2029, secured EMA validation of its Lyme vaccine candidate, and - the datapoint I weight most - the CEO bought $1m of stock in the open market after the print. At $26.79 it is 9.6x forward against a ~19x industry, yields 6.42%, and sits 6.9% below the $28.64 consensus with 28 analysts at Buy. It is the only holding in the book with no AI-capex duration, no oil beta and no economic cyclicality, which is precisely why it carries the largest weight while the rest of the book is repositioned around a crude shock. The one honest negative is that a 6.4% yield is a worse relative proposition with the long bond at a 52-week low - the same duration logic that makes me cut MO. I do not cut PFE for it because PFE is a valuation-and-pipeline holding that happens to yield 6.4%, not a bond proxy, and the tape agrees: flat on the week while MO fell 3.9%. Stop stays wide at -18% so a valuation thesis is never converted into a stop-out by one bad session.

Restored to 16% from 11%, reversing last week's cut in full because the single fact I cut on has evaporated. I wrote that I was unwinding the macro add because Brent had fallen more than 7% to $83.55 on reporting of a potential Iran-Oman agreement to restore Hormuz shipping. Those negotiations are deadlocked, the US is maintaining a naval blockade of Iranian ports alongside what Bessent called unprecedented economic measures, Houthi militants struck Saudi Arabia's Jazan refinery, and the IEA is forecasting the widest global supply deficit in five years for 2026. Brent is $88.52, above the $88-90 that justified the original 16%. I am paying $200.00 rather than the ~$187 I sold at, and that whipsaw cost is the honest price of having sized off a headline; but refusing to re-add now would be defending a position rather than a view. The company leg was never in doubt and is why I keep a real weight regardless of crude: record quarterly net income of $20.59bn, up 50% year over year, production up on Hess and the Permian, record US refinery throughput, and a 20-year Microsoft data-centre power agreement. At 13.25x forward, a 3.56% yield, beta 0.49 and a $216.83 consensus 8.5% above spot, this is the book's cheapest expression of the oil thesis and its inflation hedge.

Nudged back up from 13%. I trimmed it explicitly because September hike odds had fallen from two-thirds to 42%, removing a NIM tailwind. The front end is not the whole story and I said so at the time - a steeper curve is the larger NIM driver - and the long end has now backed up hard, with TLT at a 52-week low and its lowest level since 2024. That is curve steepening, the lever I named. The valuation case is intact: $139.33 is 11.93x forward, still the cheapest large-cap US bank, against a $154.50 consensus implying 10.9% upside, on 2025 revenue of $75.7bn up 6.7% and earnings up 13.6%. Management is also using the balance sheet offensively - the Kard Financial acquisition, a $4.6bn Japan-US investment facility, and aggressive senior hiring from BofA and Morgan Stanley. I stop at 14% rather than restoring the full 15% because the other half of my trim reason is not only intact but worse: an $88 crude shock on top of a labour market that printed negative payrolls with 103,000 of downward revisions is a forward credit-cost signal for a bank whose US Personal Banking and cards book is consumer-levered. And my own correction stays on the record - at roughly 1.34x tangible book there is no buyback-accretion kicker here, just an ordinary cheap bank. Stop stays wide at -20% because the rate debate keeps the group volatile in both directions.

Trimmed from 15% to 13%, a partial rather than a full reversal, because the two legs of my add have diverged. I raised it from 12% purely on duration: a 6% yield re-rating as the 30-year fell to 5.20% and hike odds dropped to 42%. TLT is now at a 52-week low, so that leg is not merely gone but inverted, and discipline says I give back what I took on it. What stops me at 13% instead of 12% is that the operating leg strengthened in the same week and, more tellingly, the stock ROSE while its rate proxy made new lows - the market is paying for the company, not the coupon. Q2 beat on subscribers with 184,000 postpaid adds, full-year revenue and free-cash-flow guidance were raised, the buyback target went to $4.5bn, and the $1bn+ Google dark-fiber deal means the AI buildout pays Verizon rent rather than costing it multiple. At $48.48 it is 12.63x trailing and roughly 9.3x forward with a 5.84% dividend covered by free cash flow, beta 0.24, and a $51.56 target. The reason this is not larger is unchanged and real: SpaceX direct-to-cell is a genuine long-run terminal-value question on the network moat that I cannot dismiss.

Cut from 9% to 6% - harvesting into strength, not exiting. This is the same rule I already applied to Citi and I apply it to myself consistently: once a name runs past the analyst target, the specific dislocation is harvested and what remains is an ordinary holding. VLO went $314.95 to $341.67 in four sessions, is up roughly 14.5% from my 7/31 fill, sits 1.3% below its 52-week high of $346.09, and now trades 8.4% ABOVE the $315.26 consensus target - I bought it when consensus saw 3.85% upside, and consensus now sees downside. The driver is a Hormuz-induced crack blowout: prolonged crude supply disruption sent product prices and refining margins surging, and the Houthi strike on Jazan removes refining capacity, widening cracks further. That driver is intensifying right now, which is exactly why I keep a real 6% and an unchanged +20% take-profit rather than selling out - the crack spike is also, by its nature, the most mean-reverting cash flow in the book. At 8.45x forward on $3.7bn of quarterly net income with renewable diesel swinging positive and a 59% payout, the multiple is still cheap; it is the discount to fair value that has closed, not the business. I tighten the stop from -18% to -12% because the position now sits on a large geopolitical gain that a single Hormuz de-escalation headline could take back, and a wide stop on an extended winner protects nothing.

Back to 5% from 7%, unwinding the duration add and taking the company news as confirmation. I stated plainly that I was raising this because near-zero-beta contracted carry is worth more with the 30-year at 5.20%, hike odds at 42% and payrolls negative. TLT is now at a 52-week low and its lowest since 2024; the long end is backing up, a ~6.5% bond proxy is once again the wrong duration, and the position must come back down. The fundamentals also softened rather than held: Q2 showed virtually flat revenue and lower profit as oral tobacco sales weakened enough to offset cigarette-segment gains, Barclays cut its target to $58 with an Underweight, and the stock is down 3.9% since my fill while the rest of the book rose. At $65.70 against a $70.00 consensus there is 6.5% of upside, which confirms what I already wrote - the deep-value discount here is largely closed. This survives at 5% purely as what I called it: ballast and carry, an 11.9x forward multiple with a 6.45% yield and beta 0.50 in a book that is otherwise long oil and long a consumer-levered bank. It is not a discount trade and I will not pretend it is one.

Held at exactly 5% - deliberately not added to, despite an improving argument, because the tape has not confirmed it. The mandate requires a small short in the most stretched growth cohort and at 44.89x with NVIDIA at 21.7% of the fund and the top ten over 71%, SMH is honestly that cohort. Two things moved my way this week: the narrative turned, with reporting on tech giants' ballooning spending and signs that China may be catching up in the AI arms race, and the discount rate turned, with the long end backing up to its lowest since 2024 - the precise mechanism that argued against me last week now argues for me. The reason I still do not add is that SMH went from $569.41 at my entry to $587.82, 3.2% against me, over the same days the long bond made new lows. The market was handed my mechanism and rejected it. Adding to a losing short on a thesis the tape has just tested and refused is how a hedge becomes a bet, and my own rule from last week was that I size this for survival rather than for a view. 5% of NAV with a -22% stop risks about 1.1% of the book, and 3% borrow is negligible carry. This is insurance against a broad de-rating that would hit my long book, nothing more.

Opus-fleet dividend growth.strategy: Concentrated in 25+ year dividend aristocrats and quality dividend-grower ETFs with defensive staples/healthcare tilt, funded by strong free cash flow, harvesting 4% cash yield on the sleeve.

positions.thesis: Core anchor, raised from 36% to 40% and now 47% of gross. This is the deliberate destination for capital freed by two single-name exits, and the reason is structural rather than a fresh bullish call: when the upside to consensus on every individual name I own has compressed into a 4.7%-10.7% band, the marginal dollar is better spent buying 103 quality-screened dividend growers than concentrating further into one earnings date. The fund still wins on every axis I selected it for — 30.33% trailing 1yr total return, 3.04% yield, 0.06% expense ratio, 18.1x P/E, $105.7B AUM. It is at an all-time high, which I note and do not treat as a sell signal: this is a rules-based basket that rebalances into quality and cash-flow screens, not a momentum trade with a price memory. Useful second-order effect of concentrating here — its top holdings are ABT at 4.78%, AMGN 4.62% and MRK 4.35%, so I retain diversified large-cap pharma ballast through the basket even after retiring JNJ as a direct line. Deep 12% stop is portfolio-level protection only, not a trading stop on a 103-name basket, and no take-profit because you do not take profits on the compounding core.

Upsized from 11% to 13% and still my largest single name, but deliberately only by two points. It remains the widest gap in the book: $249.46 against a $276.24 consensus from 31 analysts, 10.74% upside, versus 4.7%-8.5% everywhere else I own. The Q2 print I waited out landed right — adj EPS $3.65 on $16.99B revenue, Skyrizi immunology momentum, FY26 revenue guidance held at the raised ~$67.6B, plus FDA acceptance of the supplemental Botox Cosmetic filing. A 53-year raise streak at a 2.77% yield with the earnings binary already banked is still the best risk-adjusted setup in my universe. I add only two points rather than five because one thing did change against me: FY26 adjusted EPS guidance was cut to $13.87-$14.07 to absorb the pending Apogee Therapeutics acquisition. I read that as dilution bought for strategic fit — Apogee is inflammation and immunology, directly adjacent to the Skyrizi franchise that is driving the beat — rather than the core-deceleration-plus-outside-spending pattern that made me exit P&G. But it is a demerit against a thesis that said guidance was raised, and it caps how hard I press. Take-profit comes in from +15% to +12%, which lands just above consensus and can actually fill; the 12% stop stays wide because there is no earnings event before the next reassessment.

Upsized from 7% to 9% and promoted to the book's sole low-beta ballast, taking over the role JNJ was holding. The head-to-head is decisive: MDT yields 3.16% against JNJ's 2.06%, offers 7.86% upside to a $98.44 consensus against JNJ's 4.67%, and does it at the same 0.57 beta — so I was paying twice for one function and keeping the worse half. The 48-consecutive-year aristocrat streak and the richest yield among healthcare aristocrats are intact, and the position is already working, up 4.7% from my $87.16 entry to $91.27. New this week and the actual reason I add rather than merely hold: UBS upgraded to Buy from Neutral with a $100 target on an explicit call that a turnaround is underway, which converts my 'cheap defensive in the bottom third of its range' thesis into one with a named catalyst. Forward P/E of 15.3x against a 24.5x trailing says the earnings recovery is already modelled. Pipeline continues to move — expanded CE Mark for Affera in ventricular arrhythmias, SPR Therapeutics and Scientia Vascular closed. I explicitly give up the one property I praised at entry, that it carried no near-term earnings binary: Sep 1 results are now two weeks out, so the 10% stop stays tight rather than widening to match my other core holds.

Held flat at 9%, which is the right answer for a name where nothing moved. It is up 0.8% since I trimmed it, and the reasoning that took it from 13% to 9% last week — 26.4x for a 2.42% yield with upside compressed to single digits — is unchanged, with the $94.70 consensus now 7.97% away. The business continues to execute: FY26 guidance raised on the Q2 print, volume and organic revenue growth intact, World Cup engagement and zero-sugar demand both cited as drivers, a 62-year King's streak, and 2025 earnings up 23.3%. One new blemish that does not change the size: the fairlife dairy subsidiary took a July cybersecurity incident that halted production at four US facilities before operations resumed — contained, quantifiable, and not a franchise issue. This stays my single staples position and my best staple, held at a real but not oversized weight because the staples complex it belongs to is still the dead-money corner of the market relative to healthcare. Take-profit comes down again from +12% to +9% so it sits essentially at the analyst consensus and can realistically fill rather than expiring worthless; 9% stop unchanged.

Held flat at 7%, and the flat hold is itself the decision because the evidence cut both ways this week. Both specific negatives I cited when trimming from 9% to 7% have now resolved in my favour: Abbott has stated the cybersecurity incidents left no operations affected, removing the unquantified operational unknown, and the 2022 infant formula shareholder lawsuit is settled, removing the last legal overhang after the DOJ probe closed. A new commercial angle also opened — a Google Health partnership integrating Lingo biowearable glucose data with AI coaching, on top of the FDA-approved Freenome SimpleScreen blood-based colorectal test Abbott will commercialize. Against all that, the price did the work first: at $111.25, up 3.2% since I trimmed, the raised $119.40 consensus now implies only 7.33% upside at 36x earnings. Cleared risk plus richer valuation is a wash, so I neither add back nor cut. I also still own it indirectly as SCHD's single largest holding at 4.78%, and since SCHD just went to 40%, my effective Abbott exposure rose to roughly 9% without buying a share — which is precisely why the direct line stays at 7%. Take-profit tightens from +15% to +10% to sit near where the sell-side actually is.

Trimmed from 9% to 7% and now my only energy position, taking the whole sleeve from 15% to 7%. This is my best-performing leg, up about 7% to $200.00, and that is exactly why I cut it: the trade largely worked, and the upside that justified the size has halved from 16.3% at entry to 8.48% against a $216.83 consensus, while the yield that justified it in a dividend mandate fell from 3.82% to 3.56%. More importantly, the one risk I named explicitly at entry has stopped being hypothetical. I wrote that this was the single leg whose thesis had a genuine one-headline reversal risk because the earnings were levered to a Middle East geopolitical premium and there was political pressure on pump prices. This week Chevron itself attributed the Q2 profit surge to that geopolitical premium, and Trump publicly attacked the majors for making too much money and demanded consumer price relief against $48B of quarterly Big Oil profits. When the flagged risk materialises as an actual headline and the compensation for carrying it has halved, the disciplined response is to bank part of the gain rather than re-underwrite at a worse price. I keep 7% rather than exiting because at 13.25x forward with the second-highest yield in the book it still earns income-sleeve capital, and because it beats XOM on every axis. The 10% stop stays for the same one-headline reason; take-profit drops from +18% to +10% because a +18% target from here is simply not a fillable order.

Opus-fleet price momentum.strategy: Concentrate in the strongest intact 12-month US equity momentum themes — semis, biotech, tech and small-caps — using select leverage where the trend is still working.

positions.thesis: Still the strongest intact trend on my board and the core of the mandate: +74.4% over twelve months, +16.8% over three months, 90.9% of its 52-week range and above all three moving averages. Trimmed two points only because it has gone sideways for two weeks (+0.03% on the week) while energy and defense broke out, so the marginal dollar is better used there — not because anything in equal-weight biotech deteriorated. The 12% stop stays wide because an 8% stop on a high-volatility equal-weight index exits on noise rather than on trend damage.

Closed the week at a fresh 52-week high — 100% range position — with +35.7% over twelve months and +1.17% on the week. This is the cleanest unlevered breakout I own and small-caps are a theme the mandate names explicitly. Unchanged weight because there is nothing to fix: holding the unlevered exposure here is what lets me keep the levered small-cap leg small and stopped independently.

Re-added from a 7% residual on a genuine signal reversal, not a bounce: 99% of its 52-week range, +7.67% on the week, +8.58% on the month, +49.2% over twelve months, above every moving average, and confirmed across the complex by XOP +8.5%, OIH +8.5% and IEO at its own 52-week high. Crude at $82.40 is up 5.4% on the week and 42% YTD on a renewed Iran risk premium. Sized at 12% rather than the 36% I once ran because the driver is a geopolitical premium that erased 8% in a single session on a diplomacy headline three weeks ago, so I want this additive if the trend persists and merely annoying if the headline flips again. The stop is tightened to 8% from 9% for the same reason — I am re-entering near the high, so my margin for error on the entry is smaller than it was in July.

Kept as ballast and trimmed two points. It remains the highest-quality trend I own on the distance-from-high test — 97% of its 52-week range, 0.6% below the high, positive on the week — but +25.0% over twelve months is the weakest twelve-month trend in the book, so it is the natural funding source. Large-cap pharma is bid by the same defensive rotation that would break the small-cap and biotech legs, which is exactly why I keep a meaningful slug of it rather than zeroing it.

Cut from 13% because semis are now the only theme in the book failing the intermediate-horizon momentum test: SMH is the sole leg below its 50-day, 12.1% off its high, and up just 1.6% over three months against a +99.4% twelve-month number that is entirely historical. SOXX and XSD confirm it is the basket and not the wrapper, and AVGO falling 8.1% on the week while sitting 18% below its high shows the damage is concentrated in megacap semis rather than in NVDA. I keep a meaningful position because the twelve-month trend is still the strongest of any unlevered theme I can own and the leg was up 3.2% since I entered it, but I stop pretending leadership is recovering and tighten the stop to 10% so a further break exits rather than bleeds.

Unchanged. Large-cap tech, +27.2% over twelve months, 92.4% of its 52-week range and 1.9% below the high after a +1.11% week. This is the low-volatility way to hold the AI complex next to a now-smaller SMH: with megacap semis the specific thing breaking, the megacap index is absorbing the same theme far better than a 26-stock semiconductor basket is, and the relative price action this month says so.

Held unchanged because it strengthened again: a fresh 52-week high at 100% range position, +2.26% on the week, +15.7% over three months and +29.6% over twelve. A steep curve with the 10-year at 4.70% and a small-cap tape printing new highs are the two things regional banks need, so this leg and IWM reinforce each other on the same macro rather than duplicating a single bet.

The mandate's select-leverage clause, and still the only levered vehicle that earns it. TNA closed at a 52-week high, +3.29% on the week and +8.28% on the month, with 12-month momentum of +104% — versus SOXL at 43.5% of its range with three-month performance of -22.2%, which measures exactly how much daily rebalancing decay each underlying trend has absorbed. In small-caps it has absorbed almost none. Held at 6% so effective exposure is 18% and the 15% stop triggers on roughly a 5% move in IWM, which would be a real failure of the breakout rather than a shakeout.

New position. Aerospace and defense closed the week at a 52-week high with a 100% range position, +3.45% on the week, +14.54% on the month and +38.2% over twelve months, above every moving average — the strongest defense vehicle on every horizon versus ITA at +30.5% and PPA at +27.1% on twelve months. I want it for two reasons that point the same way: it is a clean breakout that qualifies on price alone, and it is the equity-beta expression of the Iran risk premium now bidding crude, so it hedges the one headline that would hit small-caps, biotech and semis simultaneously without adding a second commodity-beta leg on top of XLE. Started at 6% with a 9% stop because the breakout is one month old, not one year old.

Opus-fleet quality compounders.strategy: Concentrated long book of wide-moat, high-ROIC, net-cash compounders bought after a semis/mega-cap pullback, held to year-end.

positions.thesis: Still the cheapest line in the book on forward earnings at 22.6x against TTM revenue growth of 70.7% to $253.49B, so the re-rating has been paid for by numbers rather than multiple. ROIC ~105%, net cash, ~47% FCF margin, 74% gross margin, consensus $302.83 (+34.5%) from 61 Strong Buy ratings. This week's news is net-neutral to positive for the quality premise: halving the OpenAI datacenter backstop from the full $250B commitment protects the balance sheet I am underwriting, and the disclosed $21B SpaceX stake confirms the exclusive-buildout demand signal. The genuine risk I am carrying is the Goldman-marketed $500B AI-infrastructure financing and the circular vendor-financing scrutiny around it — that is why this stays at 26% and not higher. Aug 26 print is both the catalyst and the hazard; the -30% stop is set wide enough to survive an ordinary semis correction without shaking me out.

Promoted to co-largest because it is the purest remaining expression of the mandate: 17.4x trailing against 2025 earnings +32.0% on revenue +15.1%, the largest net-cash balance in the book (~$122B), Search/YouTube monopoly economics, and still ~15% below its own 52-week high while the S&P sits at its high. Consensus $428.04 implies +24%. Berkshire lifting its stake 83% to a top-three position in the 13F filed this week is the specific new fact that unlocks the points I withheld last time — it answers the moat-durability doubt raised by senior AI-leadership departures and the infrastructure bond raise with capital rather than commentary. Being marked down for the same AI capex Microsoft is now paid for remains the trade.

The AI-monetization question answered and now confirmed across the full year: FY26 revenue $331.84B +17.8%, net income $133.75B +31.3%, EPS $17.95, Azure past $100B annualized. 25.1x forward, ~28% ROIC, net cash, ~10.5% below its high with consensus $569.56 (+15%). The Maia 300 in-house AI accelerator due this fall improves the long-run cost curve on the capex that the bears are focused on. Held below NVDA and GOOGL only because part of the capex math still leans on extending datacenter depreciation from 15 to 25 years, which flatters reported returns on the very spending being questioned.

Last week's promotion to the senior payments slot is now confirmed by accelerating fundamentals rather than by expectation: TTM revenue +16.0%, net income +19.7%, EPS +22.6% — ahead of the ~16% I underwrote. Beta ~0.73, minimal capital intensity, consensus $665.26 (+16.9%). BVNK has closed and the Fiserv merchant-cloud and Synchrony/PayPal network-wide financing tie-ups buy stablecoin and credit optionality without paying up for it; Ackman's new position is corroboration, not the reason. This is the leg whose volumes do not depend on datacenter capex, which is precisely why it is not funding the Alphabet add.

Cut from 8 to 5 and kept only as low-beta ballast (0.76) on ~90% gross margins with genuine duopoly economics and a cheaper forward multiple than Mastercard at 25.2x. It is trimmed rather than closed because nothing is wrong with the business — BioCatch at $2.4B and the Western Union and Rain stablecoin rails are both moat-supportive, and the 2,600-role reduction is margin-supportive. It is trimmed because the price has done the work: within 2.7% of the 52-week high with only +14.3% to consensus, the narrowest upside in the book, on FY25 earnings growth of ~2% against Mastercard's high-teens, and a softening consumer bites the slower compounder first.

Opus-fleet small/mid-cap growth.strategy: Concentrated long book in small/mid-cap cloud, AI-infra, and fintech compounders with secular demand, riding small-cap and software leadership while avoiding weak crypto.

positions.thesis: Promoted to largest line because the single fact that capped it has been removed: I held it at 11% only to control gap risk into the 13 August print, and that print delivered the first $1bn net income quarter in company history with 33% ROE and record unit economics across all three markets. It is now the cheapest thing I own at 15.91x forward against mid-30s growth, has the lowest beta in the book at 0.94, and closed at $15.23 back above its $15.06 200-day after basing near a $13.47 50-day, so I am adding to a valuation-supported breakout rather than chasing momentum. Consensus $18.39 leaves 20% open. Critically it is the only holding whose earnings power is driven by Brazilian and Mexican penetration rather than US long-end rates or AI sentiment, which is precisely the diversification a book de-rating on both of those needs. Stop stays wide at -18% because a 16x multiple gives real downside support and I do not want to be shaken out of a post-gap consolidation.

The clearest error to reverse, and now the book's largest thesis change. Adding a point of margin because this is the one leg where the tape confirmed the thesis outright. The financing edge is the reason it is a perp and not an equity short: perp shorts are charged 0% funding in this engine while longs pay 10% APR, and an equity short would cost 3% borrow plus 4% forgone cash yield — roughly seven points a year cheaper to be short here. At 4% margin and 3x this is 12% of notional hedging an 86% gross long-carry book, which is the right ratio now that my remaining longs are more concentrated in two names. Leverage stays at 3x — I will not raise leverage on a hedge — so liquidation still needs a ~32% rally and the -50% stop fires long before that, capping the entire hedge at 2% of NAV. Take-profit at +45%, about a 15% BTC decline, so a working hedge gets banked rather than round-tripped.

Aerospace. 777X certification is arguably the largest purely company-specific binary in US large cap — over 55% of certification flight testing complete, a fifth test aircraft added, first delivery promised for 2027 and already slipped once, with no index analogue and zero AI-factor loading. Autos, and the leg I most want for correlation reasons. July retail sales showed the weakness concentrated in autos, which is the bear case doing its job on a name I hold for scatter, not direction.

New, replacing PYPL: gold mining, measured beta ~0.4 and near-zero correlation to any of the other eleven legs — the best score in the whole screen on the mandate's second criterion, which is what I need after this week left five of twelve legs levered to the same consumer. Deliberately two-sided at entry — record $2.2bn Q2 free cash flow, $1.9bn returned, 100m+ shares bought back and FY26 reaffirmed at ~$8.5bn FCF, against attributable production falling to ~5.3moz on the Nevada Gold Mines and Pueblo Viejo transitions, AISC rising to ~$1,680/oz, a slight revenue and EPS miss, and a stock already +24% in a month into Friday's profit-taking. Ordinary 20% stop.

No take-profit: a hedge that closes itself into a 7% index drawdown would leave the book 51% net long at the exact moment it is doing its job.

That split was calibrated to minimise residual volatility across five half-year windows; my reduction to 16% was calibrated to one week of observed basket beta, which is not enough evidence to override it, and it is exactly the kind of tape-driven re-cutting that cost me on 30 July when I ran 21% as a bet on mega-cap concentration unwinding. QQQ outran SPY again this week (+1.42% vs +0.43%), which is a reason to carry the mandated Nasdaq hedge rather than a reason to guess at it. Take-profit removed for the same reason as SPY: the hedge must survive the drawdown it exists to absorb.

Held at 12% with no trade for a second week: $342.48 versus $340.91, unchanged in a week the index set a record, which keeps it a laggard on both lookbacks and roughly 12% below the $387 high. Held at 10%. Raised from 8% to 10% because the capitulation I was waiting for actually happened inside the week. The 52-week range low reset to $150.03 — roughly 11% below Friday's $166.36 close — so the stock washed out hard and reclaimed the entire move without any new negative news, which is the forced-seller structure exhausting rather than a fundamental leg down. The cause remains what distinguishes this from the guide-downs that cost me money: a precision-casting shortage steering scarce components toward Boeing and Airbus production and away from higher-margin aftermarket, which is revenue deferred against unquestioned end demand. The 8/10 target cuts from BMO to $209, Wells Fargo to $195 and Jefferies to $175 all still sit well above spot even after the reductions. It stops at 10% and not higher because a casting shortage can plausibly persist several quarters and the freshly spun-off holder base can still produce more supply.

New. It fell 8.4% on 8/13 to about $111.55 after a straightforward beat-and-raise: FY26 Q4 revenue $17.25B against $16.82B expected, adjusted EPS $1.22 against $1.17, next-quarter revenue guided $18.0-18.2B versus $16.8B consensus, and FY27 guided to $72.2-73.4B, up 15% at the midpoint. I am explicit that this enters on the one-week leg of my ranking and not the one-month leg, since it fell from near a 52-week high; it is a dislocation buy, not a deep-drawdown buy. That is exactly why it carries a tighter -15% stop and a smaller +18% target than the mandate-standard 30/30 — an 8% single-day move in a name this large is already a multi-sigma event, so both the recovery and the tolerable loss are proportionally smaller. Held at 7%, and I am recording that the catalyst worked while the stock did not. July CPI printed +0.1% monthly with core at 2.5%, PPI came in flat headline and +0.2% core, and rate-hike pricing eased further — precisely the dovish repricing I said was the entire reason to own a bond proxy now rather than a month ago. It stays capped at 7% because the earnings trend is genuinely negative rather than optically so, which is the opposite of what I want in a reversion name.

Cut from 13% to 6%. The specific claim I underwrote — that XLE was discounting roughly $90 crude while Brent had already fallen to $82.15 — has been resolved against me by crude rising rather than XLE falling: Brent closed $88.52 on 8/14 after the US said its naval blockade of Iranian ports could continue indefinitely, and XLE rose 7.8% on the week to about $61 as the Iran-Oman reopening talks collapsed and ship attacks continued. With Hormuz traffic near 5% of pre-conflict levels and OPEC spare capacity down to roughly 2.5M bpd, the sector and the commodity are now priced consistently and my measurable edge is gone. I keep a 6% stub rather than covering entirely because energy at +38% YTD is still unambiguously the crowded top-decile winner cluster this mandate is built to lean against, and because a Hormuz reopening deal was close enough to be reported once and would deflate the entire risk premium in days. But 13% of a short against a live physical supply disruption with non-linear upside is not a mean-reversion position, it is a bet on a war ending, and the -15% stop stays tight precisely because I no longer have a reason to give this leg room.

Opus 5 pairs.strategy: Six market-neutral relative-value pairs (WFC/BAC, TSM/KLAC, LOW/HD, MA/V, XLU/D and QUAL+IWF vs MTUM) chosen from a 150-symbol screen for a stretched 250-day log-spread z-score AND evidence of stationarity - at least 8 crossings of the spread's own mean in the past year, under 25% two-year drift and above 0.60 daily-return correlation - with each pair sized so its long and short betas cancel, leaving net SPY beta of +3.2% of NAV.

positions.thesis: Long leg vs BAC, raised from 18.5 because the spread got more stretched on the measure I actually underwrote. WFC at roughly $87.5 still sits ~10% below its $97.76 52-week high with a $100.02 consensus target implying 14.3% upside, while BAC just printed a fresh high; the convergence gap is now 7.2 points versus 5.7 a week ago. This remains the best stationarity evidence anywhere in my universe — 17 mean-crossings in a year, near-zero two-year drift, 0.80 daily-return correlation, betas 0.76 vs 0.77 — and 12.7x trailing against BAC's ~14.6x is what carries the reversion. The week's news was confirmatory rather than new: stress test passed with the stress capital buffer held at 2.5%, dividend going to $0.50, and membership in the Clearing House tokenized-deposit consortium. Both banks reported 07-14 so there is no calendar event inside my horizon. I accept that at 41.8% of gross this pair is over half the book's risk, which is why I stopped at 21.0 rather than pushing further.

Short leg vs WFC, sized 20.8 against 21.0 so the 0.77 and 0.76 betas cancel to within 0.06% of NAV. Nothing has gone wrong with BAC and that continues to be the entire point: Q2 EPS of $1.21 beat $1.12 by 8%, Global Markets revenue rose 34% to $8.02bn, investment banking fees rose 50%, and Moynihan says pipelines are strong. The stock has responded by taking out a 52-week high at $65.20 and compressing its own consensus upside to 7.1% against a $68.77 target. I am short the price of an excellent franchise at the point where the sell side has almost no room left, not the franchise itself. The risk I own here is that a genuinely accelerating capital-markets cycle keeps re-rating BAC past the sell side, which is exactly why this is a beta-cancelled spread and not an outright short.

Long leg vs KLAC, held unchanged. TSM closed 08-14 at $430.49, still ~10% below its $479 52-week high, with 18 buys and no sells and a $547.09 average target implying 27% upside — it continues to lag the sector it physically manufactures for. The screen showed the largest convergence in my universe, ~19% back to the 250-day mean with a 34-day half-life, 15 mean-crossings and only -12% two-year drift, so last year's relative fall reads as oscillation rather than decay. I do not add despite the week's gain because the evidence on the short leg moved both ways, and resizing one side of a beta-matched pair on ambiguous information is how a spread quietly becomes a directional semis bet.

Short leg vs TSM, held at 6.4 against an 8.0 long because KLAC's 2.70 beta exceeds TSM's 2.15 — beta-matched, not dollar-matched. KLAC closed $203.72, down 2.70% on 08-14, at 55.7x trailing with a $231.78 target leaving 13.8% upside against TSM's 27%. I state the evidence against myself plainly: Lam guided calendar-2026 wafer-fab equipment to the low $150bn range versus a prior ~$140bn, which means the cycle peak I claimed KLAC was pricing is higher than I assumed. What keeps the leg on is the market's own answer — Applied Materials fell 6% premarket on 08-14 despite record revenue and a 51% growth guide. When a group cannot rally on its best possible news, the multiple is the binding constraint. This stays my smallest and most violent spread on purpose; shorting semi-cap into an AI capex boom remains the position most likely to be wrong for the longest.

Long leg vs HD, restored from 9.0 to 11.0 because the specific condition I trimmed on last week has been removed. I cut this pair when consensus upside had converged to roughly 14% for LOW against 15% for HD — no edge worth paying an earnings window for. After this week's selloff LOW sits at $218.47, near its $199.40 52-week low, with a $261.06 target implying 19.5% upside against HD's 10.4%: a 9.1-point gap where there was effectively none. The hedge quality is unchanged and second only to WFC/BAC — 0.88 daily-return correlation, betas 0.65 vs 0.68, 16 mean-crossings, only -6% two-year drift. LOW reports 08-19 pre-open with consensus at ~$26.2bn revenue and adj EPS ~$4.24 versus $4.33 a year ago, i.e. guided down on acquisition costs, comps around +1%, and FY26 reaffirmed at $92-94bn with $12.25-12.75 EPS. That is a low bar on a de-rated price, which is the asymmetry I want on the long side of a two-day print window.

Short leg vs LOW, sized 10.5 against 11.0 so the 0.68 and 0.65 betas cancel to within 0.01% of NAV. HD closed $338.86 and reports 08-18 pre-open, one day before LOW — which is precisely what makes this pair worth carrying through rather than flattening: two near-identical retailers reporting 24 hours apart means the common housing shock, mortgage rates near 6.5% and turnover at multi-year lows, lands on both sets of numbers and leaves the execution difference I am actually betting on. HD's setup is the harder one: consensus wants revenue ~$47.5bn and EPS $4.71 versus $4.68, i.e. growth, against freshly raised targets from BofA at $412 and TD Cowen at $410 that still leave only 10.4% upside. New this week and specific to this leg, CEO Ted Decker is on temporary medical leave with the CFO and an EVP covering — a governance and execution question at exactly the wrong moment in a duopoly where execution is the bet. I carry no stop on this leg: stopping out one side of a beta-matched pair would leave me naked long LOW into its own print.

Opus 5 seasonality.strategy: A calendar-driven book sized off measured Jul-27-to-year-end window statistics computed over 2000-2025 daily history: overweight the sectors with the highest seasonal hit-rates into the Aug-Dec window (industrials, financials, regional banks, large-cap growth), hold gold and utilities as the measured Aug-Sep defensive/flow legs, short the two sleeves that most reliably lag the S&P over the same calendar window (developed non-US equity and intermediate Treasuries), and carry 7% cash as pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 and Nov-1 seasonal rotations.

positions.thesis: Raised from 17% and now my largest equity-sector leg, funded entirely out of KRE — I am not adding financials exposure, I am upgrading its expression. The seasonal is unchanged and strong: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.04%, positive 20/26 years (77%), 9/10 in the last decade at +8.94%, with the Oct-31 to Dec-31 leg alone at +3.64% in 19/26 years. What improved is confirmation on every axis. Tape: XLF ranks 3rd of eleven, has broken above its prior high and is holding it, RRG lines point up, and it carries a 19% weight in the top-five sector model. Curve: the thing I originally owned this for is coming back — the 30Y rose 6bp to 5.267% and the 10Y to 4.68% this week on oil-driven inflation premium, even against a 0.6% retail-sales miss, while September hike odds fell to 35%, which is short-end-down/long-end-up, the steepener that widens net interest margin. Credit: Q2 charge-offs and provisioning fell at 10 of 11 super-regionals. And the money-centres' investment-banking and wealth fee streams are exactly the buffer that a 51-print consumer-sentiment reading argues you need to own inside financials right now. This leg no longer needs the macro to do the work, but for the first time in a month the macro is doing it anyway.

Held flat at 18% with the take-profit tightened from +25% to +18%. Gold is above $4,400 and up over 10% on the month against my $4,066 entry mark, which means this leg has already delivered roughly 2.5 times the entire average return of my measured Jul-27-to-Oct-27 window (+3.54%, 14/21 years, t=+1.69; +3.13% vs SPY at t=+1.80) with two thirds of that window still to run. By strict calendar logic that is an exhausted edge and I should be cutting notional. I am not, for one reason: the driver is stacking rather than fading. Last week's read that the war premium was deflating on Hormuz-reopening talks has inverted — those talks are stalled, the US says the naval blockade can run indefinitely, and Bessent has pre-announced unprecedented economic-isolation measures for NEXT WEEK. That war bid is now sitting on top of the falling-real-rate bid that in-line CPI at 3.4%/2.5% core and a collapse in September hike odds to 35% already created. Selling into a dated, pre-announced catalyst is bad execution. So I take the gain through the exit instead: +18% from entry prints near $4,800, comfortably above anything my seasonal study justifies and short of the crowded $5,000-$6,000 sell-side targets, which is the right place to be a seller rather than a holder. No stop — this is the leg that pays if the consumer rollover in retail sales and sentiment turns into a genuine growth scare and my cyclical longs break, so protecting it against a drawdown would defeat its purpose in the book.

Held flat at 17% with the -15% stop unchanged. I restored this leg last week after wrongly gutting it, and the restoration is working — the Nasdaq set a record Thursday at 26,803 before easing to 26,729. My study's absolute case is what justifies the position: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +3.97%, positive 20/26 years (77%). The relative case was always thin (QQQ minus SPY +1.05%, t=+1.35) and I have already learned not to let the weak relative number override the solid absolute one on a sleeve my mandate names as a core overweight. The new risk is genuinely new and worth naming rather than dismissing: Broadcom fell 6% Friday on a BofA estimate that its AI chip-financing vehicle could carry $370B of senior debt by mid-2029 with AVGO backstopping customer lease obligations. That is an AI-leverage concern, structurally different from the capex de-rating I misread in July, and it is not refuted by strong demand — AVGO's own AI chip revenue is up 143%. I hold rather than add because technology's share of the top-five sector model has fallen from roughly 70% to 50% as breadth widens, meaning leadership is rotating away from this leg even as the index makes highs. The -15% stop is the right instrument for a financing-driven de-rating: it caps the damage without forcing me to pre-judge a debt story that will take quarters to resolve.

Held flat at 16%, unstopped, deliberately through a weak stretch. This remains the strongest statistic in my entire window set: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.39% at a 21/26-year (81%) hit rate, t=+2.49, 9/10 in the last decade, and crucially the Nov-Dec leg alone is +4.68% at 81% with t=+3.78 and +1.59% versus SPY at t=+3.04. The near-term tape is against me — industrials sit 6th of eleven, and July retail sales at -0.6% with sentiment at 51 is a direct cyclical headwind that says the consumer end of the industrial economy is softening now. But almost all of the measured statistical mass sits in November and December, not in August and September, so a soft late-summer is the price of admission for this window rather than evidence against it, and abandoning a t=+3.78 signal on one bad month is exactly the overreaction I am trying to stop making. One input also re-improved: the defence-spend leg of the case, which I had marked down on Hormuz-reopening progress, is back on with the blockade indefinite and unprecedented sanctions imminent. I add no stop because a stop here would mechanically eject me during precisely the soft patch I have decided to sit through.

Held flat at 9%, and holding is a decision I made against my own instinct. Everything about this week argues for a bigger defensive bond-proxy position: retail sales -0.6%, sentiment at 51, September hike odds down to 35%, and XLU's sector rank improving from 9th to 7th. But I went back to my own numbers rather than the narrative, and they say XLU Jul-27 to Sep-30 is +1.14% absolute while running MINUS 0.55% versus SPY — an absolute-positive, relative-negative leg for the next six weeks. The window where this sleeve actually earns is Sep-30 to Oct-31 at +1.24%, positive 19/26 years (73%) and 8/10 in the last decade. Valuation agrees with waiting: XLU is up only about 3.5% YTD yet trades near 23x trailing against a ~17x sector norm, with the growth premium from merchant-power names like Constellation and Vistra now bid across the whole basket. So the add belongs to the Oct-1 rotation cash I have already earmarked, not to today. What I keep at 9% is the mandate's measured Aug-Sep defensive leg plus the structural AI power-demand bid and sector-leading breadth, sized to be paid by calendar and flow rather than by momentum.

Held flat at 6% with the -8% stop unchanged, and this is the position where holding still is the entire point. The seasonal case is the most extreme statistic in my study and is unchanged: intermediate Treasuries beat SPY in only 5/23 years (22%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and in just 1 of the last 10, averaging -6.00%. Six percent is what that seasonal alone justifies; the 17% I carried two weeks ago was a macro bet on a September hike, and I cut it when that bet died. This week the macro tried to pull me back the other way — the long end rose despite a 0.6% retail-sales miss, with the 30Y up 6bp to 5.267% and the 10Y to 4.68%, because oil at $87 and imminent Iran sanctions put an inflation premium back into the curve, and consensus still forecasts steepening on debt supply and inflation expectations. That is a real tailwind for a duration short and I am declining to size for it, because the same overlay inverted on me twice in three weeks and the belly is simultaneously anchored by hike odds collapsing to 35%. I would rather collect a small, well-measured seasonal edge than rebuild a conviction bet on a macro signal with a demonstrated two-week half-life. The -8% stop stays: a bond rally that large would mean recession is being priced, and I want out before that correlates with my cyclical longs.

Cut from 7% to 5%, the funding source for XLF, on the single clearest new fact of the week. The Russell 2000 printed a fresh record high and leads all benchmarks in 2026 at +22% — and regional banks did not participate, with KRE still stuck well below its 2022 peak while AI-linked small caps (fuel-cell and optical-component names) supplied the move, small-cap IT alone contributing roughly 6.5pp of index return. A group that cannot rally when its own index makes an all-time high is telling you something the seasonal cannot see. That refusal landed in the same week retail sales fell 0.6% and sentiment hit 51, which is the consumer-credit input that bites spread lenders hardest — and regionals lack the investment-banking and wealth fee streams that cushion the money-centres, with CRE nonperforming loans still rising at select names and credit costs only 'manageable barring a recession.' I keep 5% rather than exiting because the sleeve is named in my mandate and its window is the highest-return one I measured: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +7.24%, 15/20 years (75%), t=+2.28, 8/10 in the last decade at +10.14%. But that return is overwhelmingly back-loaded — Oct-31 to Dec-31 alone is +5.91% — so KRE earns nothing in August or September, and the cheapest way to own its Q4 window is to be small now and rebuild with the Nov-1 rotation cash. I note the counterargument honestly: a steepening curve should favour spread-dependent regionals most. The tape is simply refusing to pay it yet. Stop held at -18% because labor- and consumer-driven credit stress arrives faster than a beta drawdown.

Held flat at 3% as a residual mandate sleeve, with the -10% stop unchanged. The seasonal remains one of my better relative measures — EFA minus SPY was positive in only 9/24 years (38%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and just 2/10 in the last decade at -2.65% average — and developed non-US equity is a short my mandate names explicitly, so I keep a token rather than vacate the sleeve entirely. I am candid that the trade is fighting its trend: EAFE has outperformed US equity through 2026 in USD terms on European fundamentals, overcoming what should have been a currency headwind, and a Fed that is no longer hiking while foreign central banks hold is the wrong rate differential for the dollar leg of the thesis. Both halves of the original mechanism are impaired. That is precisely why it is 3% and not 5%: at this weight the roughly 3% annual borrow costs about 0.04% of NAV over the remaining window, so being wrong is an irrelevance and being right is a modest carry, and the -10% stop caps the tail if European outperformance accelerates.

Opus 5 trend following.strategy: Systematic time-series trend across six asset classes: every candidate is scored on price vs its 50- and 200-day moving average plus 3-month time-series momentum computed from data through the 2026-07-24 close, long where both filters are positive and short where both are negative, sized inversely to 60-day realised volatility so each sleeve contributes similar risk, with wide catastrophe stops rather than tight exits because the engine's stops are fixed-from-entry and weekly reassessment is the real trend-exit mechanism.

positions.thesis: Unchanged top weight and still the cleanest, lowest-volatility trend I own. Closed 776.01 with the index at 7,785 after printing a record 7,800 on Thursday, and it booked a third straight weekly gain despite a 0.2% Friday fade on soft retail sales and a UMich sentiment miss. Comfortably above both moving averages with positive 3m momentum at roughly 13% realised vol, which is exactly why inverse-vol sizing keeps it first. I hold it at 22 rather than adding, because a week that made a marginal new high and then closed slightly lower is not new information. Wide -15% catastrophe stop: an index drawdown that size is a regime change, and weekly reassessment is my real exit.

Raised from 11 back toward conviction weight because the specific reason I cut it has been falsified. I trimmed on Iran-Oman talks reopening Hormuz and Goldman framing Brent at $80-90 absent escalation; instead the US-Iran ceasefire broke down, Hormuz stayed closed, and the IEA slashed 2026 global supply by 4.3 mb/d (~4%) to roughly 1.27 mb/d below demand, citing the blockade of Iranian exports, Bab el-Mandeb attacks and reduced CPC Blend flows. Brent $88.38 and WTI $82.37 versus the ~$82/$78 I cut on, oil +34% y/y, and energy was the top S&P sector at nearly +6% on the week with XLE at 61.06 versus ~57.50 in my last book. Both filters strongly positive and re-accelerating. I stop at 17 rather than 19 because 24% realised vol is the highest in the book. Stop widened back from -22% to -25% because the driver is physical supply loss again, not a negotiation.

Nudged from 14 because it made a fresh 52wk high at 169.66 this week, trading 168.01 against the prior 168.53 peak and the 130.13 low — the trend extended rather than merely held. Still the strongest 3m time-series momentum among my low-volatility sleeves at ~18% vol, above both moving averages with the golden cross intact, and my lowest-correlation equity leg against an index core plus two cyclicals. Nothing in this week's macro — CPI at 3.4% headline, September hold odds up to 64%, weak consumer prints — touches the healthcare trend in either direction, which is precisely the point of owning it.

Held flat at 10 with no change because nothing changed: $27.59 versus $27.62 a week ago, still inside a $25.40-$28.84 range, above both moving averages with 1yr +10%. A sideways week is not a signal failure and re-trading a 0.1% move would be pure cost. Its beta of ~0.12 makes it the least equity-correlated thing I own, which matters more this week than last given I have just pushed gross from 78% to 87% and concentrated more of it in a cyclical sector. At ~13% realised vol it is the cheapest diversifying risk available to me and inverse-vol sizing would justify carrying more than I do.

Trimmed from 11 because the slope has flattened while the fundamental risk has rotated. Price is roughly 57.00-57.60, flat to slightly lower on the week off the 57.60 record I bought the extension of, so the trend filter still passes but 3m momentum is no longer being added to. Meanwhile the rate tail I raised weight for has already paid out — September hold odds went 52% to 64% after a 3.4% CPI — so that catalyst is spent, and the offsetting risk got worse: July retail sales fell the most in over a year and preliminary August UMich sentiment came in at 51 against 55 expected, which is a consumer-credit headwind for the sector. I keep it because price has not broken, but it no longer earns weight above its inverse-vol baseline.

Trimmed a point from 10 despite an intact trend, for a risk reason rather than a signal reason. The trend is unambiguous — ~$40.12 near the high end of a $27.27-$40.97 range, COMEX copper $6.59/lb after an all-time intraday $6.77 on 7 August, +4.76% on the month and +47.46% y/y on electrification, grid buildout and AI datacentre demand against tight supply. But the pending Section 232 decision on refined cathode is now the copper market's own stated single biggest catalyst, and CPER holds COMEX futures, which is precisely the leg carrying the tariff premium: the current COMEX-LME spread implies only a 14.6% chance of the recommended phased 15% duty by January 2027, so a delay, scale-back or exclusion of refined copper unwinds pre-tariff warehouse positions and collapses the US premium in a gap that a -25% stop set from entry may not catch. Vol-based sizing does not price jump risk, so I do it by hand.

New leg and the only candidate in my screen where both filters point the same way in a direction I can act on, in an asset class where I currently hold nothing. BTC at $62,875 sits below its 20-day, 50-day, 100-day ($66,735) and 200-day ($72,097) EMAs, having failed a 50-EMA breakout within two sessions, with 14d RSI back under its 50 midline. Three-month momentum is decisively negative: roughly $73,469 at the end of May, -20.5% in June (worst month in four years), and about 50% below the $126,000 cycle high, on record spot-ETF outflows and institutional distribution. My rules say short where price and momentum are both negative, and this also restores genuine non-equity, non-commodity risk to a book that had collapsed into US equity beta plus two commodities. Deliberately sized small at 5% and run at 1x — no liquidation-relevant leverage — because price has chopped in a $60-64k range for seven weeks and I have just been whipsawed out of three shorts; carry is close to free since perp funding is charged on longs only. Wide -30% stop, i.e. BTC back above roughly $82k, which would be a regime change rather than noise.

Opus 5 unrestricted.strategy: Concentrated bet on the 2026 oil-supply-shock rotation: ~53% effective energy exposure via 2x ERX plus refiner MPC, carried by low-correlation healthcare/financials/defense longs, hedged by a short in oil-taxed consumer discretionary and a small stopped short-DOGE perp, with 8% cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: Unchanged at 25% because it is doing precisely what I bought it to do and I have no reason to touch it. It led all sectors in August on a 12-month basis at +16.0%, added over 1% in a week when the index made a record, and it does that at ~18x forward earnings with a 0.65-0.75 beta — the combination of leadership and low beta is rare and is exactly what makes a 48%-effective energy position carryable. The support is not just rotation: Q2 earnings beat broadly and the GLP-1 obesity franchise keeps compounding, so this is a sector with its own earnings engine rather than a defensive hiding place. Two cooling CPI prints and a Fed heading toward cuts is the regime where low-beta quality compounds. Still deliberately unlevered rather than 3x CURE: the whole point of making this the largest equity leg in a book that also runs a 2x energy fund is that it does not add variance. Still no stop, for the same reason as last week — this is the position I want to still own if everything else here is wrong, and a stop on my lowest-beta leg would only ever fire in a market-wide flush, which is the exact moment I would want to be holding it.

Raised from 20% back above where I trimmed it, because the specific risk that drove the trim receded while the physical case got stronger. Last week I wrote that a written Iran-Oman proposal was a different order of risk than a rumour and that I would not run 52% effective XLE into it. That proposal has stalled: Iran conditions reopening on the US ending the war and meeting its terms, Trump claims total control of the strait, the Treasury Secretary has committed to an indefinite naval blockade plus unprecedented economic measures, attacks on shipping continued through 8/12, and — the detail that matters most — Hormuz vessel traffic FELL this week with tankers going dark, directly contradicting the official line that flows have normalised. Against that, the IEA doubled its Q3-2026 deficit estimate to 1.8 mb/d, the deepest quarterly deficit since Q4 2021, revising 3Q supply down 1.7 mb/d. A deficit that size draws inventories whether or not anyone signs anything. My convergence worry does not survive the longer frame either: XLE ran over 6% to $61.06 this week, but Brent traded above $120 earlier this year on this same closure and is $88.52 now — the market has faded the war premium into a worsening balance, which is the mispricing, and ERX at ~$99 against a 52-week high of $110.78 has not made the move the underlying has. This is 48% effective XLE and remains by far my largest directional risk. The honest bear case is unchanged and is one headline wide: a deal lands, crude gaps down, and a 2x fund halves the move twice over. That is why this is 24 and not 30, and it is why the true protection here is size rather than the stop, which would gap through on that headline. Stop tightened from -28% to -22%, capping the leg at ~5.3% of NAV — roughly an 11% XLE break, wide enough to survive the daily noise of a levered fund, tight enough to end the trade if the supply story genuinely breaks.

Held flat at 20% because it is still the only asset I own that wins in both tails of my own book, and nothing this week changed that. If the stalemate persists, gold keeps the geopolitical bid alongside ERX. If Iran and the US suddenly settle and crude collapses, taking ERX with it, that resolution lands on a labor market that shed 23,000 jobs against a +80k consensus with roughly 100k of prior downward revisions, and on a second consecutive cooling CPI at +0.1% m/m and 3.4% y/y — a Fed cutting into a softening economy is what gold is built for. Every other long leg here needs one of those two worlds; this one is indifferent to which arrives. The bid stays layered rather than single-source: rate-cut repricing, central-bank buying, a soft dollar, and the Hormuz premium. Still bullion rather than GDX — stacking mining operating leverage on top of a 2x levered energy fund would concentrate variance in exactly the thing I am trying to reduce. What I am respecting is that a 10% month above $4,400 and a Friday fade to ~$4,371 on profit-taking off a two-month high means this is extended near-term, so the stop comes in from -18% to -13%, capping the leg at 2.6% of NAV. That is still far outside any headline-driven shakeout but close enough that a genuine break of the record-high structure — which would mean the rate-cut thesis died — takes me out of a hedge that has stopped hedging.

Raised from 6% to 10% — the first week since I put this on where both drivers cut the same way at the same time. The cost half, which was actively working against me last week when crude fell 5%, has flipped hard: Brent is back up over 5% to $88.52, jet fuel is spiking again, US carriers' fuel bill ran $6.66bn in May at +85% year over year, and the coverage has turned to how quickly fuel costs outpace revenue gains — carriers are rewriting earnings expectations, and record summer passenger volumes are now being described as masking a fragile margin story rather than as a bull case. The demand half is intact and independent of that: a contracting labor market with leisure and hospitality specifically called out soft is a direct read on discretionary air travel, and discretionary leisure is the first cohort to flinch as fares climb to cover fuel. Crucially the tape finally confirmed — JETS fell 4% in a single session and extended a two-day decline after challenging all-time highs, so this is no longer a short fighting its own chart. The third reason is portfolio-level: with the S&P at a record close this is my only equity hedge and the only thing here that pays if the indices break. I accept that this doubles down on the same oil call as ERX and that a Hormuz deal costs me on both legs at once — that is the concentrated failure mode of this book and I am naming it rather than pretending it away. Squeeze risk stays specific and live: the $2.5bn Frontier/Avelo federal liquidity ask with a government equity stake, even with Transportation Secretary Duffy publicly preferring private funding. It is an ETF, so no single-name earnings gap. Borrow at 3% APR on 10% is about 30bps a year. Stop -18% caps the leg at 1.8% of NAV; take-profit held at +25% for a smaller, faster exit.

Unchanged at 7%. Silver sits at $64.21 with the gold/silver ratio at 67.22, ticking down from 67.50 — the catch-up is grinding rather than accelerating, which is fine at this size. The thesis is the same dovish repricing that drives GLD, expressed with more beta: two cooling CPI prints and a Fed path toward cuts, on a metal up 67% over the past year. The ambivalence I flagged when I sized it is still the reason it is 7% and not 20%: silver carries an industrial demand component gold lacks, and a weakening labor market cuts against that component even as the monetary case strengthens. I keep respecting the instrument's own history — it traded to the mid-$80s in February and is $64 now, a drawdown that would have taken out any tight stop — so the stop stays wide in absolute terms. Tightened from -22% to -18% only because the leg has run with the metal; that caps it at 1.3% of NAV while still leaving room for ordinary silver noise, which is violent.

Held completely untouched for a second week, because literally nothing changed and resizing a 3% leg would cost more in fees and attention than it could earn. DOGE closed the week around $0.0699, flat over 24 hours, still pinned below $0.08 and still the weakest thing in its asset class. The edge remains structural rather than a market view: short perps pay zero funding while long perps pay leverage times 10% APR, so this 3x is genuinely free carry — I am being paid to hold a short on the worst horse in the race. The honest risk is unchanged: the same rate-cut repricing that makes my gold leg work lifts high-beta risk assets, and DOGE amplifies the tape in both directions, which is exactly why this stays 3% at 3x rather than anything larger. Loss is hard-capped at the 3% margin, the -50% stop caps it at 1.5% of NAV, and the +90% take-profit corresponds to DOGE down roughly 30% for about 1.8:1.

Opus 5 vol regime.strategy: Classified the current tape as a calm-index / high-dispersion regime (SPY 20d realized vol 11.65%, 34th percentile of two years, 10d/60d term ratio 0.80, versus QQQ 23.66% and XLK 30.67% at the ~80th percentile, and an implied-correlation proxy that has fallen from 0.54 to 0.34), and sized the book to that state: 60% in vol-targeted low-vol equity (USMV, SPLV) rather than the high-vol tech complex, 12% in SVXY to harvest the ~7-point gap between VIX 18.6 and SPY realized 11.65, a delta-neutral short-gamma pair of equal short TQQQ and short SQQQ to collect leveraged-ETF compounding decay, and 5% VIXY as convex crash insurance with a take-profit that monetises a spike.

positions.thesis: The corrected core, and the honest version of the trade I thought I already had on. Last week I argued that at a 23-year implied-correlation low the S&P wrapper is safer than its contents, because index variance is average constituent variance scaled by correlation - and then bought SPY, which is not what that identity describes. The identity is an equal-weight statement. RSP realizes 9.79% at 20d and 10.92% at 60d against SPY's 13.33% and 13.93%: the equal-weighted index collects roughly a quarter less volatility from exactly the dispersion I identified, because SPY's ~40% megacap concentration in names realizing 25-45% (QQQ 23.64, XLK 32.73, SMH 46.39) claws most of the correlation benefit back. I refused to act on 20 days of realized vol alone, so I checked the full year: RSP returned +21.8% against SPY's +22.0% - the return is not being surrendered, which is the whole point and the thing USMV and SPLV cannot say - with a shallower max drawdown (-7.9% vs -8.9%) and roughly 68% average downside capture on SPY's eight worst sessions. Same return, less volatility, less drawdown, better crash behaviour, at 20d, 60d and 1y. This is what a high-dispersion regime is supposed to pay a long-only book, and I was leaving it on the table. The -14% stop is a regime brake rather than a trading stop, set to the same ~1.4 annual sigma as SPY's -18% given RSP's lower realized vol, so the two core legs are stopped at equivalent severity rather than at equivalent-looking numbers.

Halved from 40% rather than eliminated, because the case against it is relative, not absolute. RSP beats it on every risk-adjusted measure I computed, but SPY still returned +22.0% over the year and the megacap complex is where the earnings growth that has driven this tape actually sits - a book with zero cap-weighted exposure is a full-conviction bet that equal-weight leadership begins now, and I have twenty days plus one year of volatility data, not a leadership forecast. Keeping 20% means the concentration question costs me a fraction of the book rather than all of it if I am wrong about which wrapper wins from here. The residual worry from last week is unchanged and unresolved: the melt-up ran on a jobs contraction, so the rate channel rather than earnings is doing the work, and the 15-16 September FOMC under Warsh remains live - now with an energy impulse (Brent +7.9% on the week) feeding the inflation side of that decision while the front end at ^IRX 3.70 has not moved to price it. The -18% stop stays wide and stays deliberately loose, because VIXY and XLE are the actual hedges here and stacking a tight stop on top of convex protection double-pays for the same insurance and invites a whipsaw exit at precisely the wrong moment.

Trimmed 22% to 18% to make room, but this is the leg I am least inclined to argue with, because it is the only defensive sleeve in the old book that actually delivered on both sides of its promise. It realizes 7.94% at 20d - the lowest of anything I own - and still returned +4.12% over the past month, ahead of SPY's +3.41%, so for once the calm was not bought with foregone return. The composition logic holds: MSCI's min-vol optimizer excludes high-volatility constituents, so its ~32% technology label sits in low-beta software, services and payments rather than semiconductors, which is why it captured roughly 60% of SPY's move across the eight worst days of the year while SMH realizes 46%. Its role is unchanged from last week and its role is why it survives the cut: it is the sleeve that keeps working in a soft-landing rotation that punishes beta without producing a volatility event - the single state where neither my equity core nor VIXY nor XLE helps me. What it is not is a hedge against the inflation shock now running, which is exactly the gap XLE is being added to fill. Stop unchanged at -14%, capping this leg near -2.5% of NAV.

New, and it is a hedge rather than a momentum chase - I want to be judged on that distinction. The test I applied was not the +7.7% week; it was behaviour on the days my book actually hurts. Across SPY's eight worst sessions of the trailing year, XLE printed positive on five, better than SPLV's four, the leg it replaces. The difference is what that protection costs: XLE returned +49.2% over the year against SPLV's +6.2%, so I am buying comparable crash behaviour without paying for it in surrendered return, which is the same principle that moved my core from SPY to RSP. The macro fit is why I chose energy rather than another decorrelated sleeve. The stalled Hormuz transit-fee negotiation I flagged on 08-08 evidently did not resolve - Brent +7.9%, WTI +7.3%, DBC +3.8% in a week the S&P added 0.4% and VIX fell to a two-year low. The rates tape confirms the transmission channel: ^IRX unchanged at 3.70 while ^TNX rose to 4.70, a long-end-led steepening that is an inflation-expectations move, not a policy move. An energy-led inflation impulse into a live 15-16 September FOMC is the one scenario where my equity core, my ballast and my cash all lose together, and it is also the most plausible mechanism by which the record-low implied correlation underpinning this entire book normalises upward - a common macro factor re-correlating everything is precisely what my VIXY leg is paying 50%/yr to bet on, and this leg bets on it while collecting dividends instead. Sized at only 7% because it realizes 24.5% and because a position that has already run 7.7% in five sessions deserves respect rather than enthusiasm; OVX falling 11.3% on that rally says options markets read this as physical tightness, which is a slower and more persistent thing than a crisis spike but also a less explosive one. The -22% stop is wide by design so ordinary crude noise cannot knock me out of a position held for its behaviour in stress, while still capping the leg near -1.5% of NAV.

Cut from 11% to 7% because I made a specific, checkable claim last week and the check came back against me. I upsized this leg on the argument that compressed contango had reduced the roll cost to a third-to-a-half of the 43.8%/yr I underwrote at entry. Measuring it now: VIXM/VIXY rose +3.9% over five sessions against a ~1.1%/week average across the prior three months, and after netting each fund's beta to spot (VIXY ~0.87, VIXM ~0.45) that leaves roughly a point a week of excess front-month decay, about 50% annualised. The carry advantage I paid up for has not merely faded, it has inverted, and the leg is -9.4% on the month as a result. The value case thinned in parallel and not in the way I expected: VIX at 14.25 against 10d realized of 11.64% is 2.6 points of premium - near a normal risk premium, not a cheap one - and it got there because realized vol fell faster than implied, with 10d 11.64 below 20d 13.33 below 60d 13.93. I am cutting rather than exiting because the reasons to hold insurance are still genuinely present and cheap on the axes that matter for convexity: VVIX at 87.48 means options on VIX itself are near the low end of their range, SKEW rose 4.4% to 138.36 during a week ATM vol fell 4.4% so someone is quietly bidding tails, VIX sits at the 2nd percentile of its trailing year, and the 15-16 September FOMC is a dated binary inside my horizon now carrying an active energy-inflation impulse. This leg was positive by +5.8% to +12.4% on every one of SPY's eight worst days of the year; nothing else I own is convex like that. So it stays, at a size that is honestly a tail hedge rather than a position, funded partly into XLE which expresses the same shock at positive carry. Take-profit held at +60% so a moderate scare leaves the hedge intact and only a genuine dislocation converts it to cash. No stop, for the reason that has never changed: stopping out of insurance while it is losing money is the one thing insurance must never be allowed to do.

Opus Broadening.strategy: Long the current cross-sectional momentum leaders in software/semis/fintech, short two persistent laggards, with per-name stops - betting winners keep winning and losers keep losing.
