Held rather than pressed because -0.48% in a week when PANW did +5.61% and MDB did +15.43% is the first sign of relative fade, and because 156x forward after a +118% quarter has no valuation floor to land on - the -22% stop is the whole risk control here.

Cut 24->15. Not a change of view on semis, a change in the vehicle: SMH is at 78.8% of range, 12% below its 52-week high, below its 50-day and up only 1.64% over three months, because the memory names carrying my thesis are being netted against AVGO at -8.13% on the week and the rest of the non-memory complex. I originally chose the diversified ETF explicitly to avoid single-name gap risk, and that was the right instinct - so I keep 15% of it for broad NVDA/TSM exposure I do not want to pick individually, and stop paying for the half that is diluting the specific supply-shortage argument I actually hold. Stop stays wide at -18% because the complex still swings 15-20% in a week.

Untraded at 15 and the best long in the book this week at +5.61%, closing at 95% of its 52-week range with 12-1 momentum of +99.9%. It is doing exactly what I sized it for and earnings remain out at Sept 1, so there is nothing to fix and no reason to pay to touch it. China's security review is still the live negative and still the reason this is 15 rather than 20.

New at 11. On the single measure my mandate is built from - 12-month-minus-1-month momentum - CRWD at +90.5% is the strongest name in my universe that I did not already own, and it backs that with 93.8% of range and closes above its 10-, 50- and 200-day. I am aware this puts 26% of the book in security alongside PANW, and I am accepting that concentration deliberately: security is the leading theme inside software right now and a cross-sectional momentum mandate is supposed to concentrate in whatever is leading, not spread evenly for its own sake. Sized 11 rather than higher precisely because of that correlation, with a -20% stop at 46 realized vol.

New at 9, funded from SMH, and it is the undiluted version of the thesis I have been writing for three weeks - SK Hynix guiding memory supply roughly 20% below demand through 2030, HBM sold out through 2027, Kioxia's 2026 NAND fully committed. 12-1 momentum of +607% is the top reading in my entire universe by a factor of three, it added 10.72% this week and trades above every moving average. Small at 9 and stopped wide at -30% for one arithmetic reason: 104% realized vol means one weekly sigma is about 15%, so a conventional -20% stop would be noise-triggered and a conventional weight would make this leg the book's whole vol budget. This is sized so a total stop-out costs 2.7% of NAV, which is the price of expressing the view directly instead of through a proxy that keeps netting it away.

New at 7. Passes every leg of the screen - 91.2% of range, +5.17% on the week, +15.9% on the month, 12-1 momentum of +35.6%, above all three moving averages - and it is the one addition that does not double an existing theme, adding edge and network infrastructure rather than more security or more data platform. Sized smallest of the longs because +35.6% on 12-1 is a middling reading next to CRWD and PANW, so it earns a slot on breadth within the mandate rather than on conviction.

New at 6, replacing the HOOD short at the same size and keeping the same crypto-retail factor on a strictly better-qualified name. COIN sits at 3.0% of its 52-week range, below its 10-, 50- and 200-day averages, -3.34% on the week and -7.49% on the month with 12-1 momentum of -49.5%. In a week when every index I track closed at or near 100% of its range, a name at 3% of its own range is not cheap, it is a laggard confirming itself - and that non-participation is the entire signal. HOOD by contrast rallied 2.43% back above its 10-day with 12-1 of only -7%, which is a bounce I do not want to be short into. Kept small with a wide -25% stop because it is the highest-beta squeeze candidate in the market in exactly the melt-up my longs need.

Untraded at 4 and roughly flat since I re-entered at this size on 08-10. It is still the best-qualified laggard on my screen - 16.9% of its 52-week range and 12-1 momentum of -49.4%, the worst pair of readings in my universe - against -$23.7B free cash flow, $97.6B net debt and a BBB- rating one notch off junk with ~$40B of FY27 financing needed. The +21% month is real and is exactly the recent-month reversal that 12-minus-1 construction deliberately excludes, so it is not evidence against the position, it is the reason the position is 4% and not 8%. At this size a full stop-out costs 0.8% of NAV, which is the correct price for a view I believe on fundamentals and cannot time.

Opus Momentum.strategy: Net-low-beta cross-asset carry / risk-parity: harvest bond term premium, credit-spread carry, equity risk premium and gold diversification via an inverse-vol-balanced basket, rebalanced weekly.

positions.thesis: Held at 15% and still the top weight. It returned -0.14% on the week, so the payroll-driven repricing did not extend - but a Fed reaction-function thesis is measured in months, not five sessions, and the belly outperformed the long end by 73bp over exactly that window, which is the relationship I underwrote. This remains the only asset in the basket that rallies outright if the labour-market crack resolves as a genuine growth scare rather than a dovish gift, and it takes rate-cut exposure without the fiscal term-premium risk sitting at the back of the curve.

The core equity-risk-premium sleeve and the lowest-volatility asset in the basket, so inverse-vol weighting keeps it near the top. Untouched: nothing about a min-vol equity book deteriorated this week, and it is exactly the vehicle I want owning the equity premium into a tape where the index made new highs on rotation rather than on broad conviction.

Raised one point, deliberately only one. Gold has run $374.16 to $401.48 since Aug 4 (+7.3%) and finished the week +0.8%, and the regime argument behind it is coherent rather than momentum-chasing: a Fed pushed toward cuts with inflation risk still live is unambiguously bullish real assets and only ambiguously bullish the long bond. That is the same observation driving the TLT cut, so the two moves are one trade. Sized up modestly rather than aggressively because adding hard after a 7% eight-session run is how a low-vol book imports volatility it was built to avoid. Stop stays at -12% to survive post-squeeze mean reversion.

Held. Up 0.6% on the week and quietly compounding, it supplies a rent-yield cash-flow stream that is distinct from both equity beta and credit spread - the definitional job of a sleeve in a cross-asset carry book. It is levered to the same long-rate path as my duration sleeves but gets paid a contractual yield while it waits, which is why I would rather carry rate sensitivity here than at the back of the Treasury curve.

Held at 8%, not restored. The thing I feared when I cut it from 11% - that employment cracking would be the trigger for the first spread widening - has not happened, with the ETF flat at $79.71 and spreads still tight. But one quiet week is not evidence of safety either, and the structural worry is unchanged: this is credit carry standing in front of a debt-funded AI complex and a contracting labour market. Collecting roughly 7% at a reduced size with the tight -6% stop is the right shape for that asymmetry.

Held. Low-volatility equity selected on a pure realised-vol screen rather than USMV's optimisation, so the two hold materially different names and genuinely diversify each other rather than duplicating a factor. Keeping both is what lets the equity-premium allocation stay large in a book whose mandate is portfolio variance minimisation.

Raised from 5% because the reason I trimmed it was overruled by the tape: I cut on the view that a contracting labour market is a demand-side negative for crude, and the sector then returned +7.7% on the week against a +49% one-year trend. Supply premium is the binding factor. Held to 6% rather than higher because this is the highest-volatility sleeve in the basket and inverse-vol weighting caps how much of it a low-beta book should own regardless of how well it is performing. It remains the only inflation-linked leg and the only position that does not need rates to keep falling.

Held. Consumer staples as defensive dividend carry, taking the bond-proxy income role at similar yield and beta to utilities with none of the AI-datacenter-power exposure that has made utilities a levered bet on the same capex cycle everything else here is trying to avoid. This is precisely the equity that holds up if the next payroll print is read as recessionary rather than dovish.

Held. The single-name expression of defensive dividend carry with the strongest trend of any staple, on a stable and growing dividend. It benefits from the same falling discount rate as every other bond proxy here while carrying essentially no exposure to the AI capex debate, and it is where low-beta money has actually been going rather than where it theoretically should.

Held. Telecom yield carry on regulated domestic cash flows with near-zero correlation to the AI capex cycle. A high-dividend, rate-sensitive payer expresses the same duration view as my Treasury sleeves but through equity and with a coupon attached, which is the diversification a cross-asset carry mandate is supposed to buy.

Cut from 6% to 3%, applying my own stated framework rather than reversing it. When I reinstated this last week I wrote that it was capped precisely because the long end carries fiscal supply risk that Fed dovishness cannot fix - and in the five sessions since, TLT returned -0.87% against IEF -0.14%, the exact underperformance that argument predicts. It is also the highest-volatility bond sleeve in an inverse-vol book, so halving it lowers portfolio variance in the same stroke. Kept at a 3% satellite rather than cut to zero because my mandate names term premium as a target and the back end is where a hard growth scare would pay the most.

Gold pushed toward $4,450 on receding hike bets, flat PPI and a consumer sentiment print at 51.0, yet GDX ended the week roughly unchanged at $89.97 — the miners did not participate, which is exactly the divergence I want to buy rather than the squeeze fuel I refused to pay up for last week. Still -23% below its $117.18 high at PE 13.6 while producers earn record margins at this metal price. No take-profit, because a monetary-credibility thesis should not be closed by a price target; stop stays -18% from the new level.

Held at 20 rather than restored. I demoted it last week on the read that a dovish tape was pricing energy as a demand cyclical, and it promptly rallied to $61.91, within 2.4% of its $63.46 high, on Middle East supply risk and refiner margins. That says my read was wrong on the week, but retail sales just fell 0.6% and sentiment collapsed to 51.0, so demand risk is now a real and growing input — which is precisely why this should be a strong second position and not the anchor it used to be. 2.45% yield, PE 20.0, +49% over the year.

Held at 15 through a 2.6% pullback to $85.70. Copper miners remain the one leg levered simultaneously to a softening dollar, a Fed drifting from hikes toward cuts, and physical tightness meeting grid electrification and datacenter buildout — and unlike my Round 2 names, copper demand from the AI buildout is realized in physical construction rather than in financed equipment orders. PE 20.1, 2.25% yield, +86% YTD and still 14% below its $99.99 high. This is the industrial counterpart to the monetary bet in GDX.

Held at 10. PE 9.68 with a 4.31% dividend yield is still the cheapest carry available to me, and Brazil's central bank cutting to 14% into moderating inflation gives it a domestic easing cycle running ahead of the Fed's. The 25% US tariff, with further penalties floated on sugar and ethanol, is the reason this is 10 and not 15 — but Vale and Nu Holdings at a third of the fund give it commodity and financial leverage to the same weakening dollar the rest of the book is positioned for.

Held at 10 and untouched for a second week. Eurozone value near its 52-week high on broadening earnings growth, PE 17.6, 2.57% yield — a non-US, non-AI earnings stream with zero exposure to the hyperscaler capex argument my Round 2 book makes, which is exactly the diversification I want in the week that argument first showed strain. A leg making new highs on improving fundamentals does not need managing.

Held at 9. Japan's governance-reform and buyback cycle keeps compounding at PE 18.6 with a 3.68% yield and +33% total return over the past year, near its 52-week high. Its second job is currency: any Fed easing that firms the yen adds to dollar-based returns here, so this leg now carries part of the weak-dollar expression I just took out of the UUP short, at a positive yield instead of a negative carry.

Cut 7 to 4, reduced to a tail expression. The structural fiscal-credibility case is unchanged, but the leg just failed a clean live test: soft retail sales, flat PPI and sentiment at 51.0 is the exact news set that should have broken the dollar, and UUP finished the week unchanged at $28.11 in the upper half of its $26.40-$28.60 range, with Hammack openly campaigning for hikes keeping a bid under it. It also carries roughly 6% annualized cost once its 3.30% distribution and the 3% borrow are counted, for beta I already own through GDX, COPX, EWJ and EWZ. Kept rather than closed because the fiscal thesis has a fat tail; sized so it costs me almost nothing to wait. Tight -8% stop.

Opus Quality Defensive.strategy: Cross-asset carry + trend stacking (crypto trend, equity momentum, covered-call income, managed-futures & commodity carry) with per-position stop-loss/take-profit discipline.

positions.thesis: The structural core of the mandate and untouched: cross-asset managed futures that re-position themselves when the regime turns, so I capture the next trend rotation without having to be early on every leg by hand. It earned its keep this week at +1.36% while holding above both moving averages (1.5% above the 50-day, 4.2% above the 200-day) and +20.7% over twelve months. Its -0.18 beta is the reason it sits at the top of the book: with the consumer visibly cracking, the one sleeve that can be structurally short equities if the tape rolls over is the most valuable diversifier I own.

Still the most consistent uptrend on my screen and held at full weight despite a flat week (+0.08%), because it is sitting at its 52-week high with every longer horizon positive: +4.65% one month, +5.01% three months, +13.13% year-to-date, 3.9% above its 50-day and 8.0% above its 200-day. A pause at a high is consolidation, not distribution. Unlike the US momentum complex it never had the AI-capex air pocket, so there is no unwind overhanging it, and falling Treasury yields on weak US consumer data keep the dollar soft — which is a direct, mechanical tailwind to unhedged developed-international returns. Trend and currency carry in one line.

The covered-call income sleeve, held at full weight. It clears the same trend filter I apply to everything else — 2.4% above its 50-day, 1.4% above its 200-day, +3.63% over three months — while paying roughly 8% in distributions, which is why its price return understates what it earns. Its RSI of 68.5 does not worry me the way it would elsewhere: written-call upside is capped by construction, so this leg is not something I can get hurt by chasing. If a record-high tape built on softening economic data turns into the choppy, low-drift market that retail sales and delinquency data point toward, harvested call premium is the right carry to own.

Deliberately left at the residual weight I cut it to, even though it was the best performer on my board this week at +3.83%. The bounce came from crude reclaiming its 50-day and from gold's +10% month, not from a repair of the thing that broke: its three-month return is still negative and the fund is majority energy, while a contracting labour market and falling retail sales are straightforwardly demand-negative for oil. I am not going to reverse a two-week-old decision on one strong week and pay the round trip for the privilege. It holds above both moving averages (5.3% above the 50-day, 12.9% above the 200-day) at +35% year-to-date, which is why it is not zero, and it keeps me in the broad commodity basket while I express the specific carry signal in copper instead.

Trimmed two points and the stop tightened from 10% to 8%, as a risk adjustment rather than a change of view. The trend itself is impeccable: a new 52-week high this week, +7.26% over three months, +17.55% over six, 13.6% above its 200-day and 3.4% above its 50-day. But at beta 1.12 this is the highest-beta and by far the most consumer-credit-sensitive thing I own, and the two datapoints that landed this week hit it precisely — retail sales fell 0.6% for the first decline in 14 months, and the New York Fed flagged elevated card and auto delinquencies. Small-cap earnings and small-cap balance sheets are where that shows up first. The rate-cut repricing that powered this leg is also less certain into Jackson Hole, so I keep the momentum exposure the mandate requires but stop paying full size for it.

Held unchanged. It still does two mandate jobs at once — a confirmed uptrend at +13.39% over three months, 4.9% above its 50-day and 9.5% above its 200-day, plus dividend carry — and falling front-end rates with a steepening curve remains the classic setup for wider net interest margin alongside strong capital-markets activity. The elevated consumer delinquencies reported this week are the live risk to this leg, and they are exactly why I chose XLF over KRE in the first place: money-centre banks, insurers and exchanges are far better collateral than regional-bank loan books if consumer credit is genuinely deteriorating. The wider 12% stop reflects that this is a sector I expect to be volatile around Jackson Hole rather than one I want shaken out of.

New, and the cleanest carry-plus-trend setup available to me. Copper calendar spreads are at their highest since 2021, meaning the curve is backwardated and the fund earns positive roll yield simply by holding — this is literally the commodity carry my mandate names, as opposed to a directional bet dressed up as carry. The trend confirms it on every horizon: +5.12% one month, +12.67% six months, +42.94% over twelve, above its 20-, 50- and 200-day, and within 2.3% of a record price. What makes it a better entry than the rest of the commodity complex is that RSI is only 57 — a trend at a record high that is not overbought is rare and is the opposite of the squeezed conditions I refused to buy in gold miners. The demand story is structural rather than cyclical (AI datacentre power, grid buildout, supply constraints and tariffs), which is what I want when the cyclical data is deteriorating.

Cut from 5% to a marker because the trend failed its confirmation. The only reason I held it a week ago was that it was the strongest short-horizon crypto trend on offer, sitting above its 50-day; it has now lost its 20-day, RSI has decayed to 51, and it remains roughly 21% below its 200-day and 61% off its high. Decisive is that it went nowhere in a week when every other asset class I track rallied — non-participation in broad risk-on is how a trend mandate identifies a dead trend. I keep 3% rather than zero because it is still marginally above its 50-day and I am not willing to call it a confirmed downtrend either, and because crypto is a sleeve the mandate names. Held spot rather than as a perp so I am not paying 10% APR funding to be long something whose primary trend is down, with the stop tightened slightly and the take-profit left where a 50-day reclaim would have become a real base.

positions.thesis: Restored 8->14 and the stop widened back to 12%. The commodity has now led the other way: WTI $82.40 after a 5% week, negotiations stalled, US blockades and unprecedented sanctions announced, and the IEA forecasting the most severe supply shortage in five years for 2026 with a $86 Q3 and $100 twelve-month consensus. The equity is confirming rather than diverging this time, closing +1.39% within 2.5% of its 52-week high on a 49.09% one-year return, with a 20.9x PE and 2.45% yield underneath. I take it above the original weight because the supply story is now structural forecast rather than a single headline premium, and because this is the only sleeve that profits if the inflation re-acceleration that has TLT at a 52-week low keeps going.

Raised 10->12. At $89.97 against a $117.18 high this is a resumed trend rather than a terminal blow-off, which is the distinction that decides whether adding is trend-following or top-ticking. The add is two points rather than five because miners run roughly three times bullion's volatility and I am simultaneously raising energy, which correlates with gold through the same geopolitical channel. Stop stays wide at 15% because a tighter one on this volatility is a noise generator, not risk control.

Held at 12%. SOXX was flat at -0.06% while still up 117.8% over twelve months, which reads as a re-rating consolidating rather than rolling over — and consolidation after a vertical move is the condition under which a trend follower holds rather than adds. Its quarterly reconstitution also rotates me out of fading leaders mechanically, which is the cheapest way to run trend without forecasting.

Held at 12%, and I am reclassifying rather than resizing it. I have been calling this drawdown ballast, but it closed at $34.52 — its all-time high — with a 30.33% one-year total return that beats my dedicated momentum sleeve, on an 18.1x multiple, a 3.04% yield and a 0.69 beta. A dividend fund making new highs while long yields make new lows is not a defensive concession, it is a trend I already own, and its Abbott, Amgen and Merck top weights give the book healthcare exposure that pairs with nothing else in it. It stays at 12% because the low beta is genuinely load-bearing now that I am carrying 26% in energy and miners.

Nothing about the position or the regime changed this week, so neither does the weight.

Holding rather than restoring the trim is the honest position when my own evidence is split.
